text: SSH is the standard way to log into a remote Linux machine over the network and get a full command-line session on it, as if you were sitting right at its keyboard. Everything travels encrypted — the login, every command, every byte that comes back — which is why it replaced older, unencrypted tools like Telnet decades ago.

Connecting is one command: ssh user at host, over port 22 by default. A password works, but it's a secret typed and verified over the network every time, and the exact kind of secret an attacker can brute-force by guessing repeatedly — which is why production servers lean on something stronger.

ssh-keygen generates two related files at once: a private key that stays on your own machine, never shared, and a public key that's safe to copy anywhere. The math behind the pair is the entire basis for how key-based login proves who you are without ever sending a secret over the wire.

For key-based login to work, the server needs your public key in one specific place: a file called authorized_keys, inside a hidden dot-ssh folder in your home directory on that server. ssh-copy-id does this in one step. The permissions matter — SSH refuses an authorized_keys file writable by anyone but its owner.

Once your public key is installed, logging in no longer asks for a password — the server challenges your client to prove it holds the matching private key, and your client answers automatically. That's safer for three reasons: nothing secret crosses the network, the key is effectively impossible to brute-force, and revoking access is one deleted line.

This is directly how you'll connect to almost every cloud VM ahead in this course — AWS, Azure, and GCP all let you upload a public key the moment you create a virtual machine, and from then on, your private key is the only way in. Next up: once you're logged in, where to actually look when something on that machine breaks.
